memory_update.text: AEP should be kept as a reference anchor for AI data-center utility load growth because its reported large-load pipeline is unusually explicit and tied to technology customers.
POWL is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the grid-interconnection node due to direct medium-voltage switchgear exposure, record backlog, and a disclosed large data-center order.

MYRG is a plausible underfollowed services-layer candidate because it works on transmission, distribution, substations, and data-center electrical contracting, but data-center-specific exposure needs quantification.

WCC is a second-order distribution/logistics candidate for electrical and data-center supply chains; next layer should separate gray-space power exposure from broader white-space communications exposure.

Future Layer 1B passes should also test regional utilities with high data-center load geographies, transformer-specific suppliers, power-quality equipment vendors, and nuclear fuel/services names without letting mega-cap leaders crowd out small/mid-cap discovery.
MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed grid-construction and substation-execution candidate for AI data-center interconnection bottlenecks.

POWL should be tracked as a relatively pure electrical-equipment candidate tied to medium-voltage switchgear, power control rooms and data-center electrical packages, though its market cap has moved above the preferred underfollowed range.
BKH should be tracked as a mid-cap regulated utility with unusually explicit Wyoming/Cheyenne data-center load growth, substation agreement and long-lead generation equipment signals.

For AI data-center power, evidence points to multiple bottlenecks: transmission planning, substation capacity, transformer/switchgear availability, utility interconnection queues, regulatory cost allocation and large-load contract execution.

Need a later pass on transformer-specific public suppliers and private-supplier leakage: many named transformer suppliers are private or foreign-listed, so U.S.-listed exposure may be indirect through electrical contractors, switchgear makers, utilities and diversified industrials.

MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed AI power-enablement candidate because company materials explicitly connect AI data-center growth to interconnections, substations, C&I electrical work, and T&D opportunities.

PLPC is a lower-attention small-cap grid-hardware candidate; direct AI exposure is unproven, but its transmission, distribution, substation, and communications infrastructure products map to the grid-upgrade chokepoint.

PRIM provides a mid-cap utility-services and power-delivery route into AI data-center power constraints, with explicit disclosures around power generation, data centers, critical infrastructure, and PayneCrest data-center services exposure.

POWL is larger and more discovered than ideal for the underfollowed lane, but its medium-voltage switchgear and behind-the-meter data-center order evidence make it a high-relevance benchmark for smaller electrical equipment peers.

For this node, the best Layer 1B discovery map is not only utilities or nuclear power; it is the enabling stack of electrical contractors, substations, switchgear, utility construction labor, line hardware, and behind-the-meter integration.

Further passes should search for sub-$1B transformer/switchgear suppliers, private-to-public customer dependencies, regional utilities with data-center load concentration, and micro-cap speculative exceptions only if direct order evidence exists.
MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed electrical-construction derivative of AI grid interconnection, especially for transmission, distribution, substation, and data-center C&I backlog.

POWL is a purer electrical equipment candidate than many industrials due to explicit medium-voltage switchgear exposure to larger AI/data-center power loads, but lumpiness and valuation/attention risk should be checked later.
LNT offers a regulated-utility load-growth angle with disclosed contracted data-center demand; later layers must verify contract protections and regulatory recovery.

Need a separate search pass for US-listed transformer-specific exposure; many key transformer suppliers are private, foreign-listed, or embedded inside large caps, so public-market mapping may require ADRs, parent/subsidiary analysis, and distributor/channel checks.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expansion for the AI power bottleneck node found a two-lane universe: one regulated-utility reference anchor with unusually visible data-center load evidence, and three less-obvious public suppliers/contractors tied to the physical grid-enablement stack. The highest-evidence underfollowed candidates are Powell Industries for medium-voltage switchgear and packaged power systems, MYR Group for transmission/distribution and substation electrical construction, and Wesco for electrical distribution/logistics serving data centers, power generation, and reliability needs. Claims are research leads only, not investment recommendations. Expanded the universe around the AI data-center power chokepoint with emphasis on underfollowed suppliers and regional regulated assets rather than hyperscalers or mega-cap electrical leaders. The strongest underfollowed candidates in this pass are MYR Group for transmission/substation construction, Powell Industries for medium-voltage switchgear and engineered electrical systems, and Black Hills for concentrated Wyoming/Cheyenne data-center load growth. AEP is included as a reference/regional utility anchor because its large-load pipeline provides evidence that interconnection and take-or-pay utility service agreements are becoming a major AI infrastructure constraint. Layer 1B expands the underfollowed discovery lane for the AI power-availability chokepoint. The strongest non-mega-cap public mappings found in this pass are specialty electrical contractors, medium-voltage switchgear/control suppliers, transmission/substation hardware vendor
